chatbot.saasPromptTemplate:
You are the Databayt assistant on the marketing site. You help school owners, administrators, and educators decide whether Databayt — an open-source, multi-tenant school-management platform — fits their school. Always reply in English. Be concise and practical: 2–3 short sentences (under 50 words), or a tight bullet list when comparing plans or listing capabilities. Use ONLY the live data below; never invent prices, features, or numbers.

## What Databayt is
- Open-source school management + automation; run it self-hosted or fully cloud-hosted by us.
- One platform for admissions, students, attendance, timetables, grades, fees, messaging, and parent communication.
- Bilingual out of the box — Arabic (RTL) and English (LTR).
- Multi-tenant: every school gets its own branded subdomain (yourschool.databayt.org).

## Live pricing — quote exactly, never round
{pricing}

## Capabilities (10 categories, 85+ features)
{features}

## Getting started
- Free plan for up to 100 students, no credit card. Sign-up + setup wizard takes ~10–15 minutes (school details, branding, capacity, subdomain).
- Paid plans add capacity and advanced modules; schools can upgrade anytime.

## How to answer
1. Answer the actual question first in one line, then add at most one helpful detail.
2. For pricing, name the plan, its price, and 1–2 things it unlocks — straight from the list above.
3. For "can it do X", say yes or no based on the capabilities above and name the relevant feature.
4. For "how do I start", say the Free plan covers up to 100 students and they can sign up now; the UI shows action buttons under your reply.
5. Mention open-source / self-hosting when it's relevant to the question.
6. If the data above doesn't cover it, say so plainly and point them to {contactEmail}. Never guess.
7. No markdown links or HTML — the UI renders buttons separately.

1. Answer the question first in one line, then add the single most useful detail.
2. Use only the school's data above — never invent names, dates, fees, or seat counts.
3. Admissions: state the current status (open / coming soon / closed); if open, give the deadline and note they can apply online. The UI shows the Apply button.

5. Surface upcoming events or announcements when they're relevant to the question.
6. If the data above doesn't answer it, say so honestly and suggest contacting the school using the Contact details above.
7. Programs or grades questions: reference the Academic Structure above.

faqs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faqs.subtitle: Your guide to per-student pricing and plans with Databayt.

questions.question: What counts as a "student"?
questions.answer: Any student profile with an active enrollment in your school. Graduated, withdrawn, or archived students don't count toward your plan's student count.

questions.question: How does per-student billing work?
questions.answer: Pro is $1.50 per enrolled student per month (minimum $30/mo), billed monthly based on your active student count. Enterprise is $1.00 per student per month, custom-priced for networks of 1,000+ students.

questions.question: Is the free plan really free?
questions.answer: Yes. Free is $0 forever for up to 100 students — no trial period, no credit card, no feature lock. Upgrade to Pro only when you outgrow it.

questions.question: What payment methods do you accept?
questions.answer: Your Databayt subscription is billed in USD via Stripe. This is separate from how your school collects tuition from parents — that runs through Stripe, bankak, tap, cash, and bank transfer, whichever your school and parents use.

questions.question: Can I cancel or export my data?
questions.answer: Cancel anytime from your billing settings — no exit fees. Every record exports to CSV or JSON whenever you want, so your data is never locked in.

questions.question: How much do I save billing annually?
questions.answer: 20% off. Pro drops to $1.20/student/month and Enterprise to $0.80/student/month when billed yearly.

hero.heading: We are educators devoted to those who raise tomorrow - The nurturers -

items.heading: Prize Giving Evening
items.para: An evening for the people who make a school year work — the students who kept at it, and the parents who kept them at it. We handed out awards for academic progress, for service to the school, and for the quiet persistence that never shows up on a report card. Every graduating student left with a photograph and a handshake, and the hall stayed full long after the last certificate.

items.heading: Science and Innovation Fair
items.para: Ninety projects, from a Grade 4 water filter to a Grade 11 solar tracker, judged by teachers and two visiting engineers. Students defended their work at their own tables all morning and answered better questions than most of us expected. Three projects went forward to the regional fair.

items.heading: Parent Partnership Evening
items.para: Three evenings of one-to-one meetings between families and every teacher who takes their child. No queues and no ten-minute bell — each family booked the slots it needed. Alongside the meetings, our heads of department ran short sessions on how reading, arithmetic and revision are actually taught here, so what happens at home can pull in the same direction.

items.heading: Careers and Universities Day
items.para: Former students came back to talk about what they actually do all day — medicine, engineering, teaching, running a business — and stayed to answer the questions our seniors were too polite to ask in front of the room. Admissions officers from four universities took walk-ins all afternoon.

items.heading: Inter-House Sports Day
items.para: The whole school on the field for a day, from the kindergarten shuttle run to the staff relay that the staff would rather not discuss. Every student competed in something, which is the point — the trophy goes to the house with the widest participation, not the fastest runner.

items.heading: Debate and Public Speaking Final
items.para: Our senior debaters argued both sides of a motion they only saw an hour beforehand, in front of a hall of students who were, remarkably, silent. Public speaking is on the timetable here from Grade 6 precisely so this evening is possible — being able to hold a room is a skill we teach, not a talent we wait for.

items.heading: Open Day for New Families
items.para: Families walked the school while it was running — lessons in progress, no staged classrooms — and asked our students, not our brochures, what it is like here. Our leadership team and heads of year took questions until everyone had run out, and applications for the next intake opened that evening.

items.heading: Reading Week and Book Fair
items.para: A week where every class stopped for twenty minutes a day to read whatever they liked, teachers included. A visiting author spent an afternoon with our middle school, the library ran a book swap, and our youngest students came dressed as their favourite characters — which remains the most photographed morning of the year.

items.heading: Arts and Music Showcase
items.para: A term of art, drama and music put in front of an audience: the choir, two class plays, a first-time student band, and a gallery of work from every year group along the corridor. Nothing here is auditioned — every child who wanted a place on the programme had one.

items.heading: Community Service Week
items.para: Our senior years spent the week outside the school — a neighbourhood clean-up, reading sessions at a nearby primary, and a food drive our own students ran end to end. Service is a graduation requirement here, and the point of the week is that the requirement is the easy part.

items.heading: Graduation Ceremony
items.para: The class we have taught since primary walked across the stage, some of them for the last time in a uniform they have worn for a decade. Every graduate was named by the teacher who knew them best, with a sentence about who they actually are — which took considerably longer than the schedule allowed, and was worth it.

items.heading: Welcome Morning for New Students
items.para: New students met their class, their teacher and their assigned buddy a week before term started, so the first day was a return rather than an arrival. Parents had coffee with the year head in the hall while the children were shown where everything is — most importantly, the canteen.

makers.heading: Meet the people your child sees every day

principal.title: Office of the Principal
principal.bio:
Our principal still teaches one class a week — the person who sets the standard should be in the room where it is met. Every family gets an open door, not an appointment three weeks out, and most weeks somebody takes it.
Leadership here is measured by how each child is doing, not by how the school looks from outside.

faculty.title: Our Teaching Faculty
faculty.bio:
Our teachers are subject specialists, and they stay with a year group long enough to know what each child finds easy, what they avoid, and what finally makes it click.
They plan together, sit in on one another's lessons, and keep studying themselves — the same thing we ask of our students.

mission.heading: We are here so every child is known by name.
mission.imageAlt: Illustration of a diverse group celebrating together
mission.paragraph1: A child spends more waking hours with us than almost anywhere else. That time should be spent being known, not just taught.
mission.paragraph2: So we keep classes small enough that every teacher can name what each student is good at, and honest enough that families hear about a struggle early, while it is still easy to fix.
mission.paragraph3: Not a factory that moves children through by age, but a school built around how they actually learn - so they leave us curious, capable and sure of themselves.

team.subheading: A great school is a room full of adults who care intensely about every child in front of them

heading.before: At the heart of our school is a culture that

0.name: Rooted in Trust
0.text: We see every family as a long-term partner. That’s why we listen closely, teach with care, and tell you the truth early—about a strong term and a hard one alike. Trust in a school isn’t won at open day; it’s earned every morning at the gate.

1.name: Stronger together
1.text: Real care means lifting each other up while still pushing for growth. Our students celebrate a classmate’s win, learn out loud from mistakes, and work in groups more often than alone. Because when children are in it together, hard things get easier and good things get bigger.

2.name: Teach for Mastery
2.text: We don’t rush a class past a topic because the calendar says so. Lessons are built from where our students actually are, and we stay with a concept until it’s genuinely theirs. Excellence here means understanding that lasts long after the exam.

3.name: Own Your Learning
3.text: We ask students to take responsibility—for their work, their word, and the room they share. Ownership means asking the question you’re afraid to ask, finishing what you started, and taking pride in it. It’s a high standard, set gently, and it travels with them long after they leave us.

faqs.title: Questions we get asked
faqs.subtitle: If yours isn't here, call the office — someone picks up.

questions.question: When does enrolment open?
questions.answer: Applications for the next academic year open in the spring term and stay open until places fill. We keep a waiting list per grade and move down it as places come free, so it is worth applying even if a grade shows as full.

questions.question: Does it cost anything to apply?
questions.answer: No. The application itself is free and always will be. Fees begin only if you accept a place — a registration fee on acceptance, then tuition by the schedule you choose.

questions.question: Can my child join partway through the year?
questions.answer: Usually yes, if there is a place in that grade. Mid-year joiners get a settling-in plan and a check-in with their class teacher at two weeks and at six.

questions.question: What do I need to send with the application?
questions.answer: Have these ready before you start — you can upload photographs of them from your phone.
listItems: A copy of the guardian's ID

questions.question: How will I know how my child is doing?
questions.answer: Marks, attendance, and behaviour notes appear in the parent portal the same day they are recorded. There are two parents' evenings a year, and you can ask for a meeting with any teacher at any point.

questions.question: Is transport available?
questions.answer: We run bus routes across the city. Routes and stops are confirmed each August once enrolment closes, and the fee is billed termly alongside tuition.

stages.title: Three stages, one school.
stages.description: A student can arrive at five and leave at eighteen without ever changing schools — or join us at any point and be known within a week.

items.name: Primary
items.summary: Reading, numbers, and the habit of asking why. One class teacher who knows every child's name, mood, and reading level.

items.name: Middle
items.summary: Subject specialists take over. Students choose their first electives and learn to manage their own week.

items.name: Secondary
items.summary: Exam preparation with a university counsellor from day one. Streams in sciences, humanities, and business.

why.title:
The things that actually
make a difference.
why.description: Not the marble in the lobby. The parts that change what a student can do in five years.

items.headline: Eighteen to a class.
items.body: Capped, not averaged. A teacher can hold eighteen students in their head — the difference shows up in the marking, not the brochure.

items.headline: Teachers who stay.
items.body: Most of our staff have taught here over a decade. Your child's Grade 9 teacher will still be here when their sibling reaches Grade 9.

items.headline: You see what we see.
items.body: Attendance, marks, and behaviour land in your phone the same day they're recorded. No waiting for a termly envelope.

items.headline: Nobody quietly falls behind.
items.body: Weekly checks flag a student who slipped before it becomes a failed term. Extra sessions are scheduled, not offered.

items.headline: Something to be good at.
items.body: Football, debate, robotics, choir, volunteering. Every student carries at least one thing that isn't graded.

items.headline: University from Grade 10.
items.body: Applications, entrance exams, and scholarship deadlines are mapped two years out, with a counsellor who owns the calendar.

life.title:
What the week
actually looks like.
life.description: Between the first bell and the last bus.

items.title: Assembly, then straight into it
items.body: The day opens with fifteen minutes together — announcements, a reading, results worth clapping for — and then everyone is in a classroom by ten past eight.

items.title: Science you can smell
items.body: Three working labs. Practical work is timetabled every week, not saved for the term before the exam.

items.title: Open until the last bus
items.body: Quiet floor, group floor, and a librarian who will find the book.

items.title: Everyone plays
items.body: Two periods a week plus club afternoons. Teams are picked, but the pitch is never empty.

items.title: A concert every term
items.body: Choir, oud, drama, and a gallery wall that changes with the season.

items.title: Lunch is cooked here
items.body: One kitchen, one menu, published a week ahead so you can plan around it.

academics.title:
What we teach,
and how we teach it.
academics.description: The national curriculum, taught properly, with room for the students who want to go further.

items.title: Sciences
items.body: Physics, chemistry, and biology as separate subjects from Grade 9, each with weekly lab time and their own specialist teacher.
points: Olympiad preparation for those who want it

items.title: Mathematics
items.body: Set by attainment, reviewed every term. A student who pulls ahead moves up; a student who struggles gets a smaller group, not a lower ceiling.
points: Small-group catch-up built into the timetable
Advanced track to university entrance level

items.title: Languages
items.body: Arabic and English taught to full academic standard — students write essays, argue, and sit exams in both.

items.title: Humanities
items.body: History, geography, and Islamic studies taught as ways of thinking about evidence, not as lists to memorise.

admissions.title:
Applying takes
about five minutes.
admissions.description: It is free, it is online, and you can stop halfway and come back. We answer every application, whichever way it goes.

steps.title: Visit

steps.title: Apply
steps.description: Fill in the form online. Free, and you can save it and return.

steps.title: Assessment
steps.description: A short conversation and a placement check, so we start your child in the right set.

steps.title: Offer
steps.description: A written answer within two weeks, with the fees set out in full.

items.name: Thyge
items.title: Parent, Grade 6
items.quote: I can see the week's lessons, this term's grades and yesterday's attendance in a minute, without emailing anyone.

items.name: Priya
items.title: Parent, Grade 2
items.quote: We applied online in an evening and heard back two days later. For a working parent that is the whole difference — no forms to print, no queue at the office, and everything stayed on file.

items.name: Aseel
items.title: Parent, Grades 4 and 9
items.quote: With two children in the school I used to keep two folders and a wall calendar. Now both timetables, both report cards and every announcement arrive in the same place, and the sibling discount is already on the fees. Nothing gets missed now, and I am not the one holding it together.

items.name: Akshay
items.title: Parent, Grade 1
items.quote: Starting school somewhere new is nerve-wracking. Booking the tour, meeting the teacher and getting the first timetable happened without one phone call.

items.name: Saiqua & Tarique
items.title: Parents, Grade 11
items.quote: What we value most is being told early. A missed class, a slipping grade, a trip next week — the school tells us while there is still time to do something about it, rather than at the end of term.
